blocks.text: I add one point: in the Greek copy of Tobit, chapter 2, verse 11, we read that τὰ στρουθία [ta strouthia], little birds, dropped dung into his eyes. Jerome rightly saw that this refers to swallows, and renders it thus: It happened that, as he slept, warm dung fell from a nest of swallows onto his eyes. For this is peculiar to the swallow: the mother herself either throws the droppings of the chicks out of the nest while they are small, or teaches them to void outside the nest when they are somewhat bigger. Aristotle, History of Animals, book 9, chapter 7: Καὶ κόπρον τὸ πρῶτον αὐταὶ ἐκβάλλουσιν· ὅταν δὲ αὐξηθῶσι μεταστρέφοντας ἔξω διδάσκουσι τοὺς νεοττοὺς προΐεσθαι [Kai kopron to prōton autai ekballousin; hotan de auxēthōsi metastrephontas exō didaskousi tous neottous proiesthai]. This is rendered by Pliny, book 10, chapter 33, as follows: With remarkable cleanliness they carry out the excrement of the chicks; and when these are older they teach them to turn round and discharge their fullness outside. Nor is this statement of the Arabs in Damir unlike it: ولا يلقي في عشه زبلا بل يلقيه الي خارج فانا اكبر فراخه علمها ذلك [wa-lā yulqī fī ʿushshihi ziblan bal yulqīhi ilā khārij fa-anā akbar firākhihi ʿallamahā dhālik] It does not void its dung into the nest but outside, and it teaches this very thing to its chicks when they have grown up. Something similar is recorded to have happened to Gorgias, for a swallow dropped dung on him. Plutarch, Table Talk, book 8, chapter 7: [col. 68] Γοργίας δὲ ὁ Σοφιστὴς, χελιδόνος ἀφείσης ἐπ᾽ αὐτὸν ἀπόπατον, ἀναβλέψας πρὸς αὐτὴν, Οὐ καλὰ ταῦτα (εἶπεν) ὦ Φιλομῆλα [Gorgias de ho Sophistēs, chelidonos apheisēs ep᾽ auton apopaton, anablepsas pros autēn, Ou kala tauta (eipen) ō Philomēla]· Gorgias the Sophist, when a swallow had let fall its dung on him, turned his eyes towards it and said, "This is not becoming [II, 614], Philomela." The Philosopher praises this as an apt saying in the Rhetoric, book 3, chapter 3, because ὄρνιθι μὲν, εἰ ἐποίησεν, οὐκ αἰσχρὸν, παρθένῳ δὲ αἰσχρόν· εὖ οὖν ἐλοιδόρησεν, εἰπὼν ὃ ἦν ἀλλ᾽ οὐχ᾽ ὅ ἐστιν [ornithi men, ei epoiēsen, ouk aischron, parthenō de aischron; eu oun eloidorēsen, eipōn ho ēn all᾽ ouch ho estin], for a bird, if it had done it, it is not shameful, but for a maiden it is shameful. So he rebuked her well, saying what she had been, not what she then was. Nor should anyone be surprised that the swallow is given the name Philomela, although it is very commonly believed that Philomela is the nightingale. For the matter is uncertain, and many of the ancients state explicitly that Procne was changed into a nightingale and Philomela into a swallow. I could prove this without any trouble, if that were the subject at hand. But we now hasten to other matters.
